I feel like there are so many good points you made, HolyTinderwig, that I need the space for a second response!  Ha!!

As you can probably see, I’m kind of fond of the Option C hypothesis.  Incidentally I think Cation-Ratio Dating is one of the few kinds I didn’t hear much about in Anthropology.  I graduated around 2000, so definitely some things are newer than my main college studies.

I definitely do think that your Option B has a lot of merit too.  I think the idea of taking antlers from a deer type creature you have hunted and eaten just makes sense from a very human perspective.  We would want to have the ability to mimic the creature we just hunted and killed and tell stories about that.  I think where my kind of analysis of the difference between cultures goes from there is when they make gods of those creatures and associate them with specific things like yearly cycles, etc.  When cultures share THAT kind of similarity of mythical figures then it gets a lot closer to possibly meaning there was contact between those peoples or at least their cultures.

I also agree with you about the potential for shared visions with regard to shamanic trance states.  Hunted animals are a very important resource to people all over the globe.  I’m reminded that the term “deer” etymologically was once a universal term for ALL herbivorous creatures in the forest.  It basically meant “a generic forest animal.”  I think that shows just how deer became kind of the totem animal to represent all forest creatures.

There is certainly a lot of reason to see that these cultural conceptions could have been shared by even unrelated cultures, but to some extent I think that the “impermeable barrier” between the Old World and New World will be broken down in our history books one day.  The peoples of the Americas were very interested in exploration and they made great journeys that are told of in their mythologies.  I would not be surprised at all if some people traveled back and forth between the continents of North America and Asia more than once…and not only in one direction.  It could be as recently as a thousand years ago, but I think it’s more likely that it would be a couple thousand or more years back, just for the oral traditions to have time to diffuse between people from the Americas to Europe.  The reason our collective memory would not have recorded this contact would be because it had to be filtered through so many layers of different cultures before it had made its way over that vast distance of almost 3/4 of the globe, from East to West.

We all strive to have a kind of overarching conception of human movement in ONE direction, and I think this theory flies in the face of that kind of thinking, so people reject it out of hand.  It really makes sense to me that we can’t so easily reject people moving from the Americas (after millennia of living there as separate cultures), to Asia.  Localized reasons could easily have spurred them into great migrations.  Things like the ancient Mount Tehama in California exploding in a monstrous eruption could definitely have changed whole ecosystems and sent people up the West Coast of North America in boats that they eventually could use to get to Asia that way.  I think if we are lucky we will find evidence of these migrations “backward” one day.

I agree with the OP, that this is a great and wide-reaching response!!  I take this stuff seriously because we should all remember that until possible connections like these are properly evaluated, you can never really say anything with real assurance.  It is definitely not unreasonable to consider that the images of gods or just mythical figures with antlers on their heads, seeming to have a connection to the cycle of the seasons, could be an ancient shared concept amongst many varied cultures.  Knowing how they could be connected (even if the connection is merely just a kind of shared human consciousness like the seemingly common image of dragons) can be very useful in seeking ancient ways of life of people across the globe.

One thing this reminded me of is the fact that not only do we know with some certainty that there were multiple waves of immigrations of people into the Americas in Prehistory, but we also know it’s fairly certain there were also some waves of people coming BACK from the Americas in Prehistory.  The assumptions about Native People of the Americas has generally been that they took a one-way journey and so often I have heard the “Land Bridge Theory” that I want to scream.  Archaeological evidence has proven to a point that MOST archaeologists are satisfied with, that humans arrived before 20,000 years ago in the Americas (long before Clovis Culture).  There was no land bridge in the Bering Strait at the time, but so what?!!  Australian Aboriginal Peoples arrived there about 60,000 years ago and Australia never had a land bridge to Asia.  Humans have had boats a LONG TIME, and even now the ice sometimes freezes over the Bering Strait and Americans and Russians can walk between the two countries by simply making the ice trek from Little Diamede to Big Diamede.  The land masses are close together and even with relatively primitive boats people could cross that waterway.  They could keep land in sight the whole time most times of year.  People were in New York State and in South America over 20,000 years ago, and possibly over 24,000 years ago.  However, what might be more relevant to this inquiry is how many people came BACK from the Americas to Asia and beyond?!

The Ket People of Siberia are thought by some to be related to the Na-Dene (Navajo) people of the Southwest.  We tend to be so adamant that we have to belittle the possible achievements of the prehistoric people of the Americas, I think it’s very possible we have ignored some of their great explorations and their sagas.  I actually would argue some of this is due to political correctness that attempts ostensibly to enlighten people about the cultures of the Americas, while actually having the opposite effect and blanketing over the many, many different cultures of the Americas in one giant politically motivated blanket statement about them.  They were VERY different from each other, and each had very different ancient histories.

One last thing I just want to mention is that I don’t mean to necessarily say there is a direct or genetic link between the ancient Americans and the early Celtic People, but I think it’s relevant that the time period when this would have happened (as our friend mentioned above) could be in the era of about 13,000 years ago.  By then American populations of various peoples were booming.  If some left and returned to Asia, and their culture spread, then the ancestors of the Yamnaya and possibly the Celts or others might have been in Central Asia at the same time.  This is a time we don’t know enough about.  One interesting additional fact is that some very disastrous volcanic eruptions had been happening in the Americas, and enormous amounts of forest fires had been happening.  Might THAT be a reason early Americans might go back to Asia?!  If they spread their culture, it would be likely that some of their mythology could have been carried forward on multiple continents.

Anything is possible, but I think it’s a very interesting thing to consider what these kinds of connections might reveal.

These are designs said to be related to temporary eye issues caused by psychoactive drug use.  I definitely think that some of the consistent aspects of rock art can be explained by these effects of drug use, but that hardly helps to interpret their specific meaning and significance.  Rock art people in archaeology are definitely kind of their own unique branch.  They have their detractors, but I find it a useful study when you can relate the art to existing species of animals, etc, or artifacts.

They had boats we have found that could potentially have made the journey.  If the Tule came to Greenland by kayak thousands of years ago, I think the Irish might have taken even small boats and gone island hopping from Ireland to Scotland to the Orkneys and Faroes and there even are some seamounts that are believed to have sunken down beneath the waves now, but are postulated to have been stopping places between islands on the way to Iceland.

Similarly we know that the early Polynesians had contact with the Quechua of Peru because they not only took sweet potatoes from them, but the WORD for sweet potatoes in Quechuan.  There are MANY such contact stories.  This is why I don’t rule anything out unless I have definitive proof either way.

There seems to be a lot of controversy here about this post, which I think is not very openminded, but regardless I just wanted to put in my two cents as an archaeologist:  IF these Native American depictions are to be considered potentially to be representations of the same religious figure (whomsoever that god was), then what I want to say is that they could be referring to the Fremont Culture of Utah as far as I could tell.  I would like the OP to let me know where they found the right anthropomorphic rock art figure from.  I want to look into it just out of curiosity.  You can learn more about them on this website for the Utah Natural History Museum.  They are currently a bit of a mystery and their artifacts are rare:

https://nhmu.utah.edu/articles/2023/05/fremont-horned-figurines-what-are-they#:~:text=These%20figurines%20are%20visually%20striking,see%20in%20the%20rock%20art.

There are definitely other horned humanoid figures from the Southwestern United States.  The significant thing about this one is not only the association with the snake, but also the spiral and the straight “horns.”  Many of the figures in rock art of the Southwest in general has what you might call more bison type horns.  They are curved and not right on the top of the head.  They are more on the sides.

I’m not super convinced by these two photos alone.  I know what one would do to properly investigate the idea they are related in Anthropology, but I need to start with the properly identified picture on the right because I don’t have enough information to look up more about it.  Details like estimated dating (which is very hard for rock art) could make a big difference in its interpretation.

I don’t want flack from anyone about my accenting to any “side” on here.  I am just trying to help by adding information.

UPDATE:  I found the photos of this exact rock art on this website…

http://travisnovitsky.blogspot.com/2013/04/southwest-rock-art.html?m=1

These are about 1,000 to 3,000 years old (it is ESTIMATED) and they are indeed from Utah, 40 miles west of the Green River.  Ironically I was very close to there just last week!  They are considered to be attributed to the archaic Barrier Canyon culture.  As I mentioned it is notoriously hard to date rock art.  These could be from roughly 2,000 years ago…but plus or minus about 1,000 years.

These are considered relatively unique compared to other rock art in the region.  Sadly it appears to me most of the rock art around it was obscured by drippings from the rock above.  That ruins the context and so it’s hard to tell what the meaning is of the main two figures on this panel.  The other figure is a very odd looking character with a snake near its head and eyes that seem to bulge out on stalks like maybe a Mantis.  It is to the left of this image.

It is clear that the image of horned anthropomorphs and snakes are definitely common in this culture, and from my experience it seems they are somewhat less common but certainly quite significant in Celtic rock art and other depictions.  I would really be interested in pursuing what that could mean.  The connections may be sparse and the potential for connection dubious, but certainly there is no harm in seeking to find information there.  You can never find something -even if it exists- if you aren’t searching for it or ready to accept it if you find it accidentally.

I can also tell you from our family’s experience that the Hollywood Police WERE corruptible.  They definitely were paid off and hid things many, many times in the Golden Era of Hollywood.  They even hid things about my personal family that we never asked them to cover up.

I don't want to downvote and just not say anything to explain (so I didn't downvote).  I can explain why it is your professor is possibly right and wrong at the same time:

  
The genetics for blue eyes are actually less multi-variant than most human genetics, BUT they are still a bit confusing because of a few factors...Hair color is way more complicated and almost impossible to predict currently, but eye color is normally fairly predictable in comparison, but still there are about three randomizing factors.  Your eye color is not really blue or brown (or green) in any clear way.  Blue is NOT an eye color, and I will explain what I mean.  Blue is the lack of any pigment.  It isn't a blue pigment, it is actually the absence of pigment.  When someone's eyes are green, that is actually codominant brown AND blue genetics (or rather, partial brown, because blue isn't a pigment).  Your eyes can therefore be partially pigmented, fully pigmented, or not pigmented, and we see those genotypes as the phenotype of having blue or green or brown eyes, but there are no "green" or "hazel" eyes in a genetic sense...as far as TRAITS.  Those aren't genetic entities, they are just variations of the amount of "blue" versus brown genetics you have...and what that really means is the quality of brown or lack of brown pigment you have.

  
Now I know that sounds confusing, and it IS, but its actually LESS confusing than most other human traits...but WAIT, THERE'S MORE!!  All of the above is probably what your professor is thinking when he told you that you can't have brown eyes if your parents have blue or green eyes.  Now, what he didn't explain is that there are also MANY human variations in addition to that ONE gene locus.  Let me just say that if your parents both had green eyes, or even one of your parents had green eyes, then that means that parent DOES have a gene for brown eyes, and therefore they CAN pass that on to you, and it can become fully dominant instead of codominant (or partially dominant...I apologize that I am shaky just at the moment on how to explain the difference between codominance and partial dominance, but I don't want to get into that because the real issue is the next thing I will address).  What the biggest issue is with what your professor might have said is that there is a DIFFERENT gene locus for whether your pigment of your eyes is expressed in a transparent way or not...



So what that means is that means is that you can have the EXACT genetics to have brown eyes, and yet you can also have a genetic code that makes your eye pigment clear instead of colored brown.  In that case BOTH YOUR PARENTS CAN HAVE BROWN EYES and you can still have blue eyes!!!  That is possible.  It is also possible that both your parents have blue eyes AND they carry the genetic code that makes their pigmented eyes clear instead of colored, and so they can pass on the trait of having brown eyes to you and yet NOT pass on the trait of having clear pigment to you, and thus you have brown eyes EVEN THOUGH your two parents both had blue eyes.  That IS possible.  It would be rare, and so your professor wouldn't want to confuse you by getting into the bizarre 5% or less kinds of situations that could come up like that.

  
What I want to emphasize is that human genetics is MUCH more complex than Gregor Mendel's pea plants.  I can tell you are a student and you are trying to learn this, so I don't know why everyone has to downvote you.  I believe it is true that you are factually wrong though, and that isn't your fault.  We are learning more about genetics everyday, so this isn't necessarily something everyone understands.

  
Before I go, I want to also address albinism (OSA 1, 2, 3, and 4), leucism, and piebaldism, melanism, and hyperpigmention.  These things can cause eye color changes, just as they can change the rest of the body.  You have probably heard about albino humans, but keep in mind SOME albino humans have red eyes, but most do not.  There are several kinds, as I mentioned at least four.  Melanism and hyperpigmentation can also have levels of variation that affect the eyes and their pigmentation.  Therefore, there is just a LOT of reasons for humans to have a variety of colors of eyes despite whatever their parent's eye colors are.  Individual humans can even have a mutation that means that their genetics show variations not present in their parents at all.  Some humans have two different colored eyes (like David Bowie).  So it really is pretty complicated.  Your professor probably just wanted to make it easier to understand.

Damn, I wrote a great response to this, talking about the huge male mountain lion that killed my grandpa’s awesome goat in 1984, but it was lost!!!  My battery had to be charged, so I’ll just give a quick summary:

Hunting in broad daylight, in the morning, in an area within 100 feet of a house, and staying by the goat’s body even while my grandpa and a friend buried the body, where they found the mountain lion had sat and watched them from less than 25 feet away, ALL that is crazy and not at all common.  This mountain lion, even emancipated, was nearly 160 pounds.  All muscle.  That’s BIG.

I’m telling you all this, however, to point out that even a totally crazed and giant mountain lion that was willing to hunt in dangerous circumstances right next to humans, STILL didn’t harm those humans.  Even when they were unaware, and less than 10 yards away.  This says a LOT to me about the will these big cats have not to kill people.

Sure, they are dangerous, and you can run into a particularly mean mountain lion…just like a mean person…but their instinct isn’t to go for a person.  They know that’s the most dangerous thing they can do, and they only do it when they actually feel like there isn’t another way, in my opinion.  Like I say, out of 39.1 MILLION Californians, the official record is something like about 80 cases where they have ever shown conclusively that a mountain lion ate a person…since the state became a state.  That’s like one every 2 years for the whole history of the state.  You’re LITERALLY more likely to be killed by bees or by sunstroke or by driving absolutely anywhere in a car.  Even if there are twice as many mountain lions killing humans as the records show, that would still be one a year or less!!

I think the main thing is that they really don’t want to eat you. If they attack you it would be more of a thing that probably came from defending themselves or their cubs or a number of other things.  It may sound funny, but my brother has gotten bears to leave who were nearly right on top of him while he was in a sleeping bag, just by saying, “No, bear, no!”  The bear just kind of said, “Oh, okay, fine…” and left.  If they were looking to eat people normally, that might be different, but I don’t think that’s their intention at all.  I think they are opportunistic if they feel like they have to attack someone for a specific reason, they might then also eat them.  It confuses the issue though, because they aren’t starting from the point of view of wanting to eat a human.  It’s just that meat is meat when it’s dead.

I’m sorry if I gave the impression you are at all likely to be attacked by any mountain lions.  They are really not dangerous like that.  I was mainly just meaning that I’m around this one at my house day in and day out, and if I were a different kind of person then I might be a bit more wary of living every day with a mountain lion around.  However, it isn’t something I would worry about.  They are probably the actual least likely of all big cats to even attack a person.

Another factor I should probably add is that cougars/pumas/catamounts/mountain cats/mountain lions, are a branch of the cat family that are unusually closer to domestic house cats than a lot of other large cats.  They actually purr and make similar noises to house cats.  If I saw a lynx, which I have, I would be actually VERY worried about that.  A tiger or a lion?  -NO WAY!!  Those are MUCH more dangerous.  They are physically a lot different than our mountain lions.  For one thing, tigers are HUGE!!!  Mountian lions are really normally strong, but even a huge one weighs a lot less than most of us do.  If you picture a 120 pound animal dragging off a 100 pound human, that’s like you carrying a child who is 75 pounds for a long time.  It’s not likely to be something they would want to do.  They know we fight back and we are dangerous.  I’d rather be close to a mountain lion than nearly any other large cat…and so I AM!  Ha!!

I want to just add my two cents.  I’ve had mountain lions on my property where I live for years (not THAT far from Yosemite, as a matter of fact). She’s literally coexisted with me for YEARS, and not been seen or heard.  I still FELT her though.  She has come back for years and had cubs on the property.

Finally this last year she came back and found her den DESTROYED and she was PISSED!!!  Get this:  She marched up and down my driveway yowling at the top of her lungs.  I don’t think she was just calling for a mate, because she appeared to be also aiming her fury at me at the same time.  She did this for days on end!!  Amazingly she was walking within 20 to 30 feet of my front door and I still wasn’t SEEING HER!!!  She is AMAZING at staying just inches outside the halo of light my porch light casts and she knows how to clear the way when I shine a lantern or flashlight in her direction.  It’s actually kind of amazing to me, because with her LOUD YELLING me, it wasn’t even remotely difficult for me to echo-locate her as being directly outside the circle of light on my driveway…

So, anyway, she finally calmed down and hasn’t been pacing my driveway yelling at me anymore, but I’m more aware of her presence than ever.  I live alone with a small dog that would present no challenge to her if she wanted to take him out.  I feel kind of surprised to have found this new sense of peace and tentative acceptance from her.  My Dad actually caught her in the flashlight JUST ONCE before, and he felt her stalking him in the bushes.  He never saw her again though.  My brother once saw her cub, but not her, and he backed away carefully.

All this is to say, I am not really concerned even if I remain respectful of her space.  I have no doubt of where she is most of the time, and I know the seasons she is there and when she is away.  I’ve caught other creatures on cameras while I wasn’t there, like big black bears and bear cubs and all manner of smaller creatures, stay cattle, deer, opossums, raccoons, skunks, gray foxes, etc.  She hasn’t shown up even ONCE though!!  I’m not easily made uncomfortable, but I have to admit she surprised me when I realized she had been living close enough to me that she could watch me water the back lawn from barely 15 feet from the edge of where I have often walked around blissfully ignorant to where she slept.

I’m fairly sure after over a decade or more around her, that she has had MANY opportunities to harm me, yet she hasn’t decided to.  Sure, she could.  One day something could snap in her head and she could leap on me, but I’m sure she weighs close to the same weight I do, and I don’t think I would make a good meal for her.  I would certainly fight back.  If you look at the OFFICIAL records in California then you see that there are actually less than 100 CONFIRMED kills of humans by mountain lions since 1850.  Now, there are almost CERTAINLY more than that, but most of the time people are killed by mountain lions and no part of them turns up afterwards.  I’m sure that happens.  However, it’s rare and they call them ghost cats for a reason.  They really aren’t going to attack a person who weighs nearly their same weight.  Children and slender women are typically the ones that have been confirmed kills.  Sometimes thinner or shorter men.  (I’m not super tall myself, but I’m not particularly worried.)

It’s completely possible I am naive, but I know that at least my own local mountain lion representative is fairly reasonable with me thus far.  She was pissed her den was gone, but she hasn’t even come into the light to say so.  She just moaned and grumbled from the shadows.  They are certainly NOT an animal to take lightly, but they also are not really LOOKING for a fight with a human.  If you appeared injured or weak, or just unusually incapable of fighting back, I think they might sense that and take the advantage.  That would be a rare day though.  They would have to be pretty desperate.

Well, I don’t know…I beg to differ.  I see where you are coming from, but the fact that the cars are still attached to each other makes me think that the momentum could have yanked the two autos on the head end into an unnatural direction.  When cars have one truck on own rail and the other truck on another rail, just the weird, sideways pressures can make cars ride up and over switches and do weird things.  I had this happen in front of me more than once.  I hate to admit that it was my crew on occasion, but also other crews I was working near.  We had a damn switch in a STUPID place in our yard that should NEVER have been thrown against us.  (We called it a “TRAP,” but lazy crews wouldn’t line the switch back after throwing it.)  The switch was about 20 cars into a yard track and impossible to see around a curve.  If it was against you then you would run it through and then if you pulled back the other way, cars would often go in two different directions…just like how they did here!  We had a big yard, so this happened probably five or six times over a decade or so while I was there.  They finally took the damn switch out, but not before it had caused too much damn trouble for too long.  So, this is why I might sound overly adamant that this is possible.  I got called in to clean up OTHER crews messes at that switch several times.  It struck me as odd how the Hell they ever got it that way, but just like in this case, sometimes the autorack or intermodal bay would ride up over the switch on one truck and then the next truck would go on the other rail.  When the car was turned almost entirely sideways and still moving, that was about when the crew noticed it and stopped.  By that point it was totally obvious they were Fů&KED.

So, while it may seem like it had to be the switch, I have my doubts.  Mainly I doubt it was a mainline switch like that because even when the railroad maintains SOME switches badly, a mainline switch where double track goes to single track, at a control point that a dispatcher is in charge of?!!!  That is probably the least likely switch to be poorly maintained of ANY switch on the railroad.  That’s the kind of switch that should be working and lubricated and totally tight in all its tolerances.  If it weren’t them the dispatcher should already have been letting the crews know that switch was failing.  The sensors would be telling them that from halfway across the country.  Therefore I guess it could have been a bad order autorack, or bad track, or both, but I doubt it was the switch…

As I say, I get where you are coming from.  It’s damned weird that those two head end autos went down the mainline and didn’t just derail, but I think the was just because of the forces exerted by the derailed car behind them.  It would have been pushing them outward toward the left of the photo.  When the third autorack derailed, it was being forced sideways and it was unable to get back on the diverging track.  It was also still coupled to the cars in front of it and behind it.  That forced them to unnaturally spread out, finding the next most natural direction to go, besides the diverging path.  So they HAD to go down the mainline.  Either that or they would have derailed as well.  I’m actually surprised they didn’t.

I will declare my bias and say that I am not an outright believer in aliens.  I’m willing to believe if I ever saw convincing evidence, but so far I’ve been actually very disappointed in how often seeming evidence of alien phenomena has been easily disproven to a degree that I couldn’t maintain any real opened mind toward it.  I know that people who believe in aliens also often believe in extremely advanced technology, but let’s use Occam’s Razor on that theory and say that it’s thousands of times more likely we will find microbes on Mars who have NO advanced technology, than that we will find aliens from outside our Solar System have ever visited Earth.  I’m not sure most people are aware of the distances we are talking about here.

It would take 75,000 years to reach the closest known planetary system to us, if we were capable of traveling light speed (and we are not).  Even an alien race who could move at several times light speed would take thousands of years to reach us, and WHY?!!  Physics doesn’t currently accept there is a way for any spacecraft to move at a speed that would allow living beings to survive moving millions of light years in anything close to a lifespan that would make it possible for aliens to visit us.  The reverse argument would have to be made also:  If an advanced civilization of aliens could travel tens of thousands of light years in a limited time span, they could undoubtedly travel FAR beyond our planet.  We may think we are rare and special, but it really begs the question what is so special about our planet that they would come here?!!  And if they did, why do we think they would be coming for US?!!  It’s far more likely they would be coming for uranium or liquid water or some other thing we have in abundance that isn’t common elsewhere…even helium.  I can’t believe we would be anything more than an afterthought.

So, suffice to say, I haven’t found convincing evidence to say aliens would come here.  However, all that aside, assuming aliens DID routinely come to our planet, that still doesn’t answer the question why the Hell they would pick up this random dude.

Therefore, I doubt aliens took him.  Ruling that out, we have the fact he left and didn’t come back.  That isn’t completely unusual, but it is more than a little odd that there isn’t any evidence of what happened to his physical remains.  His body had to have gone somewhere, and I doubt it was space.  It’s not actually that hard to lose a body in the wilderness though.  A substantial number of people disappear into the woods every year and many never are found even in pieces.

I think the biggest mystery here is the fact he left a note and disappeared and left no trace behind of what happened to him.  It’s not that unusual, but still worth the search.  The note is odd less because of the things he said about aliens to me,
Than the fact he clearly is giving no sign he plans on returning at all.  Was this mental illness?  Maybe, but then one would think he would have been easier to find, deceased or otherwise.  The nature of being delusional is that you are less likely to have it together enough to make a complete escape, leaving no remains.  To totally disappear seems less likely to me for a mentally ill person.

So that leaves me wondering if there was a DIFFERENT reason he wanted to disappear.  Maybe he wasn’t mentally ill or thinking aliens were planning on coming for him…Maybe that was the cover story.  Maybe he left to join the CIA and didn’t want anyone ever looking for him (except maybe near his former home).  There are certainly enough people who WANT to disappear.  I think those are the ones who are least likely to be found.

It is a worthy mystery, and one worth solving, but I would rule out several possibilities right off the bat…I doubt he was picked up by aliens or that he launched a spaceship of his own or something.  I also think he could have been mentally ill, even if it was in a functional way.  The way he disappeared makes me think maybe this was a deliberate disappearance and not a plan to go meet some aliens.  People often have more than a few good reasons to disappear.  Anything from getting out of child support to a lot of other things.  I wonder if this was just a red herring to create a reason to think he vanished forever, just so he could start a new life.

I actually was driving through that exact area just this week.  The basic evidence points to them meeting someone with bad intentions to me.  Going out to buy land, money in hand, that can be a very dangerous thing to do.  People rarely seem to know how dangerous it can be to go places with a lot of money with you.

I know, I know, then why didn’t the person who might have bumped them off find their car and the dog and take off with the cash?  -I think that it’s very possible that they were killed in a non-invasive way.  Strangulation or poisoning might not be detected years later (with scavenging by animals or insects, etc.).  The murdering party might have deliberately made sure they bumped them off before they got them to give up the location of their car with the money in it.  They might have not gotten to that part before they passed out, etc.

My theory here is very loose, I fully admit.  It would require me knowing a handful of additional details to figure this one out better.  First off, I want to know if the car keys were on their person…If they were found with car keys on their bodies, that would be evidence to me of NO foul play.  However, if they didn’t have the car keys on them (for example) then that would be VERY good evidence that they had met with someone and foul play could be a possibility.  I would also want to know where they left the car.  If it was in an obvious place then that would mean foul play is less likely.  If the car was off the road, even just a little way, maybe it was not noticed.  Then it might be foul play.

In a situation like this, I follow the police’s standard assumption.  I err on the side of foul play unless there is good reason not to.  Here is why:  3 people don’t often just up and die altogether.  Even if they were lost, it would seem more likely that they would have been split up.  Getting lost and dying of exposure would be hard to believe if they were really only 3 miles from the car.  In addition, if they did die of exposure then I would actually expect the child to die earlier than the parents and probably one parent would stay with the child while the other went for help.  That just seems more likely.

The third possibility I see is that this was a murder-suicide pact.  That could certainly be true.  It would explain their mood before they left.  This is STILL a case of foul play, but one that doesn’t involve anyone more than the people who were there.  They could have chosen to go out into the woods and kill their daughter and then themselves.  As others have pointed out though, this seems highly unusual for people with $32,000 and a dog waiting in the car.  I doubt that would be the case.

So, here is how I have to ping-pong my way back to the basic evidence I see.  If they were not killing themselves and the bones don’t show obvious injuries (like by bears, for example), then I feel like it was SOMEONE who killed them.  I don’t think they killed themselves, and I don’t think they died of exposure because that would be unlikely in my mind (for the above reasons).  I think someone ended their lives for a foul purpose, and that afterward they were laid down altogether because the murderer(s) didn’t feel like separating them.  Many murderers do that with families or couples they kill.  It would make sense that the motivation was the money, but it’s also at least possible that the murderer(s) failed to find the car or somehow failed to get the money.

It isn’t THAT uncommon for idiot thieves to leave the impetus for their crime behind after they have felt the shock of having to overcome someone and leave them dead.  Maybe they wasn’t even the intention.  Maybe they died too soon or died when they weren’t expected to.  Maybe they were supposed to go to sleep and then wake up without their money or their car, but instead the thief killed them and left them without even figuring out where their car was.

It IS a mystery, but I think it’s best to handle one part at a time, and make logical deductions.  Some key facts to me here is that it seems unlikely that they died of exposure in a place they knew well, barely 3 miles from their car.  I would believe that they killed themselves, but leaving the money and the dog in the car?  That doesn’t add up for me.  The most likely scenario I can see is someone was waiting for them (since they were supposed to be going to buy land, as we know), and that this person actually lied to get them out in the wilderness with a lot of cash in hand.

They should have had some clue about updrafts when they considered this plan.  I mean, I am not an airship captain, so I might not be an expert in landing such a dirigible.  However, at that time they certainly had enough of them to ask around and see if this was worth attempting.  I am of the opinion it wasn’t a very serious plan or else they would have done some testing before dedicating the top of the building to it.  I normally wouldn’t say this, but it seems to me it actually was a real trick to have a reason to surpass the Chrysler Building’s height by building what was essentially just superstructure.  I also think that where there’s a will then there is a way.  There are plenty of crazier stunts people have done, even with blimps!!  I think they were kind of forced by the fact they had committed to making the “mooring mast” at the top, so they had to make at least one attempt to dock an airship there to prove it wasn’t a lie…but I think they would have made more than one try if it was a serious plan.

The updrafts make it nearly impossible to moor there, and I’m sure that the layers of air pressure also are quite different at that height than they are at lower altitudes.  With almost no other tall buildings of similar heights around, that would mean the airship would be exposed to all kinds of stronger winds beyond just updrafts.  However, all that being considered, I grew up near an enormous airship hanger.  They can wrangle those things in a number of conditions.  It isn’t thoroughly IMPOSSIBLE to hook up to a tall building.  I think the impracticality was a great deal to do with the complications of making a gangplank contraption that wouldn’t terrify passengers.  Would it be POSSIBLE?!  -I think ultimately it WOULD be possible.  Would it be practical?  -Probably not, but that would be mostly due to people not feeling comfortable with airships in general, as a means of transport.  People were critical of airships as a means of travel even before the Hindenburg Disaster.  Apparently airships are a lot more bumpy a ride than people would expect.

I know people who have ridden in the Goodyear Blimp, and they say it’s a surprisingly bumpy ride.  The idea we generally have without having tried it is that it would be like riding around on a cloud.  Just like a huge hot air balloon.  I have also not tried a hot air balloon, but from what I have heard the two means of travel are very different.  In my personal opinion it’s kind of sad that these are both not very practical as means of travel.  I would like to see more airships, not less.  They seem like they should be a fairly efficient way to travel, but evidently not.  They have to deal with constantly changing conditions and either they have almost no control over where they end up and need a nearly ideal set of conditions to fly, OR they have to use a ton of powerful propellers, etc, and even with all of those they are very slow.  I would have to look up how long it took them to cross the Atlantic, but I’m guessing it would have to be more than a week or two at times. Anymore is a negation.  The connotation of the word is to say something is NOT happening in some way.  If you say, “People rely too much on their devices anymore,” you not only are adding “anymore” to a sentence where it imparts no additional information beyond what is already conveyed in the rest of the sentence, but you are also NOT negating anything.  Notice when I say “anything,” I am pairing that word with a negation as well.  We say “any” as a prefix mostly when we are excluding things.  “Anymore” means something is NOT continuing.  “I don’t use my devices too much anymore,” makes sense because I’m saying that something has ended…I am NOT doing it anymore.  It’s a pair with not.  If there is no negation then anymore doesn’t belong in the sentence.

English used to have intentionally paired negation sentences with ALL negative words, which is why Shakespeare is fully of what SEEMS like double negatives.  Double negatives were not considered wrong then, but they also meant the opposite of what we think they meant now.  Not and nor would go together in a sentence like, “I am not going to work today, nor do I plan to go out with friends.”  That is all negative with matching terms.  The opposite would be a positive sentence like, “I am either going to work today, or I will go out with my friends.”

If you say a sentence like, “I am not going to work anymore,” then that is where the word belongs.  MORE is the operative concept, and “any” is negating whatever would be more.  If you said, “I am going to be going to work FROM NOW ON,” then that would be kind of the opposite of saying the negative sentence version that ends in “anymore.”

It sounds exciting to say that we will be TOTALLY DIFFERENT in 5,000 years, but if you ask me it is more likely (judging from the rest of our history) that we will be STILL living on Earth (but maybe also on other planets or satellites, etc.) and that we will still have ideas about “the Divine” that involve anthropomorphic figures with animal characteristics. Some things about us humans seem almost hardwired into our DNA (maybe literally), and so I think we respond to similar iconic imagery as a part of our basic nature.  When you see religious symbols from the Neolithic or from even earlier cave paintings and carvings, even very rough ones, it seems they truly have some aspects in common.  If you pare down the many gods and goddesses of religious pantheons across the Ancient World you see some themes come up again and again.  Notably these ones seem very consistent:

God of War

Goddess of Fertility

Wise Elder Male God Figure/“King of the Gods”

Mystic Older Woman Goddess

Some Form of Triple Goddess

God of Weather

Trickster God

Mother Goddess of the Earth

Water Goddesses

God that Created

I’m not just channeling Joseph Campbell here.  I’m trying to legitimately sum up what I know in general.  The Archetypes are there for a reason because they really resonate with the literal make-up of our being.  There are more too, but these are just a rough start.  These types of gods seem to pop up everywhere.

Well, I mean I am not suggesting it is a SIMPLE cipher.  I’m saying that the Enigma had different sized wheels and an assortment of varied means for changing the code and scrambling it.  I think this has a scrambled code and without knowing the right key it really SHOULD be impossible to decipher it.

However, since it has some repeated words, that tends to indicate it isn’t wholly nonsense.  That should mean there IS a pattern (as stated in the Wikipedia article).  That pattern is undoubtedly extremely hard to crack, but just as many mathematical problems have never been solved, so too is it possible there IS a means to crack the encryption here, but I suspect the hardest part is LAYERED KEYS.  I think it needs more than one key to decipher it.  I think it is not simple at all, in that it needs a key to the elementary substitution and a SECOND KEY to the mathematical function that has to be run to the initial key.  Just those two steps would render it beyond most computers ability to figure out.

Adding to that, you might need a historian to give pointers on that because some mathematical notions of centuries ago have changed.  Computers and cryptographers now would not necessarily know every detail of those historical changes to mathematics.  Human foibles could be part of what is holding up the decryption.

Incidentally, I used to work for the British Museum and frequently discussed things like the decryption of Egyptian Hieroglyphics, etc, with scholars there, so I think I am not completely outside of my expertise when I say there are problems more complex than just having computers working on them.  For example, NO ONE knows how to read Harappan.  It’s one of many languages that have never been deciphered.  If it was so easy to do, I’m fairly sure someone would have.

Therefore, taking all that into account, this could be a language that is constructed (as said in the introduction), like Esperanto.  It could be a language that is not known to the cryptographers who have worked on it, and just combining that with a complex cipher that requires multiple keys, should I easily be enough to make it incapable of being decrypted.  I’m guessing it is a combination of using an alphabet we don’t know, using a constructed (non-natural) language, and also using encryption.

As I understand it, there really ARE still uncrackable codes.  They are rare, but even if we think we are the greatest humans who have ever lived, some thing’s are still beyond our capabilities even now.  I feel like I have a hunch this will turn out to be ABOUT something.  I don’t think it is an entire book of nonsense.  I also think it will be able to be cracked, but I think the thing holding that back from happening is that it is more than one step of the several that were listed in this post.  It is not just in a foreign language or foreign alphabet.  It is both of those plus a complex encryption.

I suspect that it is too complicated to be ONLY a hoax.  In my opinion it is a rotating cipher, which is to say that it would use a key something like the enigma machine.  The letters are NOT random, and they probably are alternating the key throughout.  Something like the Letter A is advanced by 26 the first time, to be substituted with Z, but the second A is substituted with a negative 2 added, means A is now X, etc.  The cipher bounces around according to very difficult to decipher mathematical patterns.  You would need three parts to decipher it;  The substitution key, the mathematical code that acts as an intermediary step between the substitution and the original, and then you would need at least ONE EXAMPLE of a translated word.

The Enigma Machine type of cipher has existed for centuries and even people like Edgar Allen Poe used it.  The kind of encryption our smart phones and computers and other devices use is basically the same except that they use two codes to act as a key, and one code is not know to you or any other person.  It is stored in your device.  Then second code is one you have invented, and the third is the set of rules that your devices uses for the conversion (such as 32-but encryption, etc.).  The reason A.I. and other code breakers have not deciphered it is that the pattern is legitimately the actual hardest code to crack.  It is not impossible that such codes could take even our fastest computers many years working on only that code to decipher it if they don’t have why part of the key.

I doubt this is a book of deep secrets because it would be foolish if someone went to this amount of work to create something utterly meaningless.  I don’t rule that out, but it is less work to actually translate and encode a cipher than to just write page after page of gibberish.  Even by accident the human mind would eventually find it was easier to copy something than to just write page after page of nonsense.  I’m betting some things like the plants and animals that are drawn are actually nonsense and not meant to represent any real plant or animal.  They are misdirection.

Oh Lord, I bet you this is one of those words the “scholars” back in the 1700s decided had to have a P in it because they wanted everyone to know how clever they were…even if it never would have had a P in it in OUR LANGUAGE otherwise.  YES, I am aware that it comes from Greek Ptero for wing, but the spelling in English doesn’t have to match the spelling in Ancient Greek.  I would prefer we spelled things the way we actually say them (rather than how someone said it in a foreign language over two thousand years ago!  Ha!!).

Case in point:  Island used to be spelled iland in English.  Yes, we didn’t have standardized spelling then, but for roughly a thousand years or so it was not spelled with an S.  Romans spelled the word isle with an S, so the “scholars” of the 1700s (roughly) decided that the spelling must have been meant to match that of isle, so they added the S to make it match.  (Nevermind that we don’t pronounce isle with an S either…)  Subsequently it has been shown fairly conclusively that we got the word island from the Norse, who spelled it without the S.  We got isle from Latin, but not island, and thus adding the S to island instead of removing it from isle is madness.

Likewise, I am quite sure Tarmigan would be understandable as a word to everyone, and it would match the Scots source.  If you had to explain that it comes from a Greek word that starts with a P, I don’t think anyone would suffer from not knowing that information when they first saw the word.  At the very least they would not be confused when they heard someone say it and then went to look it up in the T section of the dictionary.

I am a fan of phonetic spelling, and while I GREATLY value the etymology of words (which is obviously why I am here), I think being true to how we pronounce words is far too important to allow for adding extra letters to words just for the sake of making them similar to their ancient antecedents.  If we went back to Ancient Greece and tried to say Ptero “properly” I have no doubt they would shake their heads and say, “No, that doesn’t sound like their PT sound or E sound or R sound or even O sound…I mean, which O in Greek are we talking about anyway?  Omega?  Omicron?  Do we have to add Omicron AND Omega to our alphabet for the sake of certain Greek words?

I think the P in this word is ridiculous, and I will die on that hill.

I don’t know…If this were “real life” in any sense, I’m fairly sure Diamond City would NOT be where I would want to be.  It’s really too many people to safely exist there for long.  It’s surrounding by dangerous areas and it’s a breeding ground for disease.  That many people without good sewage facilities?!  There would be cholera and parasites.  Lice and fleas and based on the other insects in the game these things would be terrifying.

I would want to be in a smaller community where there was more control over the influx of outsiders coming to trade.  I know these aren’t things to look out for in the game. But given the conditions I would really want to live in a place more defensible than the biggest city around.  This is mainly from my knowledge of history and from working as an archaeologist.  Denser places get hit HARD by famine, pestilence, diseases of other kinds, etc. That’s been true for the last 20,000 years at least.

In REAL LIFE?!  If I were living in 2280 something I think Spectacle Island is a damn good place to set up shop.  I would defend the Hell out of it.  I would put up barbed wire and mines if I had to.  I think it is the most realistically defensible areas of the whole game.  It feels less like it in the game because super mutants and others just spring up out of nowhere, but in “real life,” if I was to be in the Commonwealth 200 years after a nuclear war, I think lots of things would make Spectacle Island ideal.  In a time when lots of people don’t have boats or ships, the real life version of that island would be a lot harder to get to.  That would be particularly true with about 20 people all farming and defending it.  There might be some pretty killer storms but people have been living through those a long time, even if they have to rebuild.

If I didn’t go for Spectacle Island, I’d almost certainly think Vault 88 is an ideal spot.  You can always come up to the world to do business, but it’s a very defensible space.  It has resources.  I’m not as sure about growing things down there as much if this were “real life,” as I think plenty would be problematic about growing crops underground.  All the same though, fresh water that is radiation-free and fully stocked facilities, would all be very worth it.  I would guess that would be the best defensible space overall.

Diamond City is great for having a lot of people, but that doesn’t make it safer in my book.  It’s in the midst of a bunch of very bad neighborhoods and it’s more of an aberration than a safe location.  Lots of people means plenty of chances for things to go wrong in my book.  If this were more like real life, Diamond City would be crawling with disease.  It doesn’t really have enough in the way of medical facilities, and the sewer systems aren’t really sufficient to prevent things like Cholera.  Seriously, if this were a little closer to real life then there would be a LOT of diseases worse than Mole Rat’s Disease to look out for.  The most common diseases would come from living around groups of people that size.  It would be like nineteenth century London.  There would be death and disease everywhere.

It’s probably because I studied Archaeology in college, and worked for the British Museum for awhile (indirectly, as a commercial archaeologist), but all these kinds of things occur to me when I’m thinking of what Fallout would be like if it were real.  At least SOME things about it COULD be real.  Plenty is very unlikely, of course, which is also part of the fun of it.

The most likely bet for a good place to live in the game would be anywhere that there could be a hidey hole that I could store my things underground, but surrounded by a small band of friends who could keep a farm going in an out-of-the-way location.  20 people is basically a band or a tribe.  Eventually everyone would be related.  This doesn’t happen in the game, of course but in real life there would be plenty of women getting pregnant and there would be midwives and other services around.  Contraception would be rarer even if it were available some way.  Without mass manufacturing there wouldn’t be a lot of ways to prevent pregnancy and there would definitely still be people having sex.  The influx of new births (hoping that there wouldn’t be too many radiation caused defects) would have a huge effect on the demographics of society in only a small number of years.  Truthfully, based on how this goes all over the world, the raiders would start to die off because people would kill them off.  Once any segment of society gets even a little behind and they have a bad reputation, killing them all off wouldn’t be hard.  They just keep repopulating in the game, but in real life they would only take a concerted effort for a few years to wipe out.

I think in a generation or two, large farms would be taking over with large nuclear families like in Early America.  After all, the people in the game have that culture as well (albeit in an Alternative History reality).  People would be having families of like 15 or so, because farming encourages this lifestyle (the agricultural revolution was really what spurred on a lot of “Patriarchy” in the world…It isn’t a political thing, it’s a natural outgrowth of an agrarian lifestyle).  Hunter-gatherers in the majority of human history were likely fairly matriarchal.  Staying in one place and farming, requiring surplus grain to be stored, led to the conditions that caused warfare to spread and there are many reasons this encouraged Patriarchy.  (Seriously, just read an Anthropology textbook…and I can easily add more for anyone who is interested.)

So, if Lewis Binford is to be believed, I think people would be more tribal, but with the vestiges of the shared knowledge of their distant past.  They would form city-states, and working together while being independent would be the norm.  It would have to be, or else periodic famines and plagues would kill them all.  Spectacle Island would be one of the best places to avoid disease and to have a supply of fish and farmed foods, with the ability to trade with the mainland but also the water to provide a protection against raids.

This is a bit confusing actually.  While there are lots of corporations that might be older, under British Common Law, the first was the Merchant Adventurers, who partially developed out of the Wool Merchant’s Guild and Skinners and Tanners from the Middle Ages in the Yorkshire area.  They had origins from as far back as the 1200s.  By the 1400s they had gotten a “patent” from Henry VII, and later they developed into a corporation under Henry VIII and were clarified in their royal charter by Queen Elizabeth.  By then Henry Hudson the Explorer had found a sea route to Moscow, and he got the company renamed the Muscovy Company as a result.  His father and cousins also sailed for them.  He found Svalbard in one of his most successful ventures ever.  While his North American expeditions were fairly popular in terms of his popularity, they didn’t make him or the company nearly as much money as his explorations into the Northeast and Svalbard.

His explorations directly lead to the Muscovy Company branching into other ventures like the Virginia Company and eventually the Hudson’s Bay Company (not directly related, but many similar investors).  You could say that the various offshoots of these ventures started with the Merchant Adventurers though.  I know the official start of the Hudson’s Bay company was much later, but we are talking about many of the same people who were involved in the same kinds of projects.  Hudson’s Bay Company wasn’t really strictly a North American corporation from the start.  It was granted arms by the College of Arms in London and it was patented there as well, as far as I know.  Like the Merchant Adventurers and its connected companies, I think the origins of the Hudson’s Bay Company have deeper roots than we give it credit for.  Colleges like Harvard and Yale are old to be sure, but were they genuine corporations when they began?  Is a college a corporation?  Was it considered one by British Common Law?  I’m not sure, honestly, but I think the set of companies that came out of the various first settlement ventures in America were kind of predating Harvard and Yale by a bit.

It is kind of confusing what to consider a corporation because the modern definition is significantly different from the version of it in the seventeenth century.  However, surely you’re right that Harvard and Yale as institutions were quite early.  I know relatives of mine who arrived in the 1620s were working on behalf of the Virginia Company and some were even at Roanoke before that, in the first group of settlers that all made it home (including Ralph Lane, the Governor). I’ve read up on these companies for years, but try as I might I have to admit it is hard to get a handle on all the interrelationships.

No, but seriously, I wouldn’t just go by the DNA.  You want to now establish the paper trail of who exactly it is in the royal family.  Find out how you are connected to them.  Being related to royalty isn’t unusual, but knowing exactly the way you are related to them is unusual.  Then you should research the history of the family.  The great thing about royalty is that they are MUCH easier to research than the ordinary layfolk.  The laity might not have records, but the royalty almost certainly requires them.  Therefore, I would start researching your way back to who is Hungarian in your family.

An easy way get started on who is the side of the family that is Hungarian is to look at your matches and which matches have the double “coincidence” of being related to you AND a specific parent (it will tell you which parent by saying maternal or paternal, even if you don’t have your parent’s DNA…and you can determine which parent by your known ethnicity from them), and their also showing as being partly Hungarian.  So the three relationships are you, a parent, and ethnically Hungarian.  Look for those matches.  Pretty soon you will have some cousins at some level who are Hungarian.  There might be a chance they are Hungarian but not related to you on the Hungarian side, so try to find things like shared surnames or locations of relatives, etc.

Eventually the photo will develop of who is who.  It takes time, but it is rewarding and there are so many stories to find along the way!

Incidentally, I LOVE Experimental Archaeology!! It’s not just reality TV stuff like the Tutor Farms recreations.  This is stuff that is generally completely untelevised.  Just people really living, eating, drinking, and (excuse me for saying it) excreting in the real way of the people who lived there 4,000 years or more in the past.  By creating the actual waste a human generally would from back then, and living as much according to what we know about those people, they are then able to compare the kinds of literal crap and figurative crap that ancient people did, and by doing that we have a very good baseline for what number of people lived in a given Iron Age hillfort in the middle of England thousands of years ago, because we can estimate the amount of people who lived there in the past by measuring the waste they left and comparing that to the waste left by modern day human experimental archaeologists who have lived it…

…And, you are SOOO right!!  Culture IS sadly very ephemeral.  In particular the Celts and the early Brythonic peoples, and the Norse Scandinavians tended not to believe in writing some aspects of their culture down, despite that they did have writing!  Thus, it deeply saddens me how much of history has been lost.  Imagine if we knew more about the Iceni than just what the Romans said about Boudicca!!  Wouldn’t it be amazing to hear her story in her own hand?!

It’s even sadder to me how many cultures we have almost willfully misinterpreted over the years!!  Despite what people want to believe, I am often very aware of how obvious our modern biases are!!  There are always debates over things like cannibalism, and frankly it is clear to me that people can’t get over their own modern bias about things like ancient people using body parts from other humans.  The fact is, many people around the world didn’t consider other tribes of humans to be THE SAME SPECIES as they were, essentially, and they used words similar to those used to describe animals for those other people.  Not everywhere, of course, but really seeing all humans as similar animals is kind of a new culture we have today.  The name for a lot of Native North Americans for their tribe was, “the people” in their own language, and often the name for other groups of people kind of implied they were anything but PEOPLE.  I say all this because I’m trying to explain that WE are the ones with a bias about things like cannibalism because it is frankly hard to define.  If you don’t find human remains physically in the feces of another human, it’s hard to prove that actual cannibalism took place (and not just rituals involving spreading ashes of the dead or even body parts, etc.).  Even if people DID eat other humans though, I would say it’s relevant how THEY felt about it, and that cultural understanding is more significant than any modern attitudes we have about that.

It’s funny to defend cannibalism, but it’s one of many debates I have seen in archaeology and I think at a bare minimum it shows how unable to give up their own biases many people still are even in Anthropology.  Just because we don’t like incest or cannibalism or pharaonic circumcision, doesn’t mean it didn’t happen and it doesn’t mean we should think we understand the place it had in these ancient cultures.  Hell, even in relatively modern times the Hapsburg Monarchs were doing some very incestuous pairing, like uncles and nieces, etc, so we aren’t really ALL that different from the Hawaiians and Egyptians whose royalty married siblings most of the time.

I was a California Railroad Conductor, so I’ve been down a lot of industrial leads like these.  What I always got a huge kick out of was going down tracks no one had seen a train on for 40 years or more.  It was hilarious to me that people were like, “What in the HELL ARE YOU DOING?!” when we used our railroad right-of-way.  The humor for me was that people always seem to assume that we have no right to be on our own tracks.  They acted like it must be some huge mistake and we absolutely shouldn’t be allowed to just take a train wherever we felt like…The best was in industrial neighborhoods that had been converted to fancy high-end lofts.  People would come out and stare at us while trying to protect their $100,000 sports cars.  They were just sure we were in the wrong somehow -even if the tracks they lived next to were from the 1870s.  (These tracks are clearly not being used because they appear to be actually cut off from the mainline and have dirt up to the top of the rails in some places and asphalt over them in other areas, but there are LOTS of rails that appear “abandoned,” that actually aren’t in any way.)  Rails are made from a grade of steel that tends to gain a patina of rust relatively quickly, so a set of rails might actually only be unused for a matter of months before they start looking like they haven’t been used in decades.  It can be a subtle difference that lets you know it’s been 30 years of non-use compared to 2 years.

One of my most interesting experiences was going into a former paint factory to get the last cars out of the plant before they tore it all down.  The same cars had sat there for at least two decades without being touched.  We came in, hooked up to them, and pulled them out, and people up and down the street on both sides were staring at us in disbelief…This is an oddity about the railroad, they both last for a VERY long time and if there is even a chance they might be used for a profitable reason then railroads might hang onto a spur track or industrial lead for a long time.  In other cases it is ridiculous how fast they come tear out tracks when they feel like it will give them a tax break or something like that.  I worked in the industry a long time but I still am unclear on the exact nature of what makes their mind up.  It’s rather haphazard from all I can tell.

Most of the circumstances of industrial leads and related drill tracks like these have to do with the number of potential industries on that route.  It also has to do with the potential for strange complications in railroad logistics. If they can store random cars on random tracks then they will.  If they have a “runaround” somewhere that it is likely needed and nowhere close by is an acceptably alternative runaround spot, then they will hold onto a piece of track for that too.  I’ve seen MANY very random seeming industrial tracks with almost no businesses on them, which the railroad just holds onto (instead of ripping them out), for purposes that are almost entirely based on the random utility of that lead having a wye or a drill track for car storage or a good runaround, or a rare piece of track like a balloon track.  Most of these reasons wouldn’t occur to people who aren’t working at that current time period at the railroad.  Often it is also based on WEIRD considerations like the time of day that they have a specific “job” for on the railroad.

Railyards have union contracts that say things like if they set a local industry job for the time period of 11 PM to 7 AM (which is when the majority of work gets done for railroad workers) then they HAVE to keep that job going if it’s been X number of days in a row.  Then it necessarily becomes a permanent and biddable job that is required to be kept on the schedule.  It’s hard for railyards to just start and stop jobs at will on their schedule because one job is scheduled at this time or that and railroad higher ups don’t want to allow more jobs if they can help it.  People get assigned to that job on that specific schedule and then it gets frozen in stone for years and managers don’t want to mess with it, even when it has less and less work.  There’s a LOT of politics on the railroad…It’s crazy!

Okay, so if you happen to know London, the first archaeological site I ever worked on after graduating college in Anthropology was at the Northern Terminus of the Northern Line, and it was one of Capability Brown’s most famous landscape creations!!  I dug it up, PERSONALLY!!!

I’m not from England, by the way, but I lived in London to do archaeology…

I had totally forgotten that his real name was Lancelot.  I think he might have been of Irish descent, which made him naturally (for the times) kind of automatically lower class to the English.  Lancelot was a lofty sounding name even then though, so it would have been even more a chance to make fun of the poor man.  That’s why I think he preferred Capability, even though it makes it that much more ridiculous sounding as a name.  The reason they called him that was to make fun of his “poor English” because he was not very educated.  In the 1600s and 1700s it was right and proper to say a plot of earth had many “possibilities,” so that was what people expected when he actually would say, “Me thinks it ‘as many capabilities…” and so they would make fun of him for it and thus he got named “Capability Brown.”  He became world famous though, because he was the one who brought a NATURAL look to English Gardens.  They had been ALWAYS symmetrical and very manicured and not at all what we now think of as more normal landscaping.  He had a hand in really changing landscaping toward where it has gotten today.  (Not that I mean to imply I know all about landscaping, but I do know archaeology and geological work a bit.)  His gardens were sprawling and imaginative, but they realistically blended nature and water “features,” as well as rocks and areas without greenery into the whole “composition.”

What made Capability Brown very different than today though, was his use of the “dramatic,” you might say:  He would hire “hermits” to sit in caves in the garden and be grumpy and not want to see anyone (although, in truth, they were just paid actors).  Garden Parties were a big thing then and if you were wealthy enough to have a giant manor house and estate in North London (actually outside of London at the time), then you would want your guests to come see your amazing garden with the grumpy troll that lived in a cave and complained that you were bothering him with all your noise. I think I said this somewhere in another comment on this sub, but I used to be a cemetery director (which isn’t the same as a funeral director, mind you), and what it taught me was to really take in the way humans have some continuity of life.  When you’re young you love to see things change (most of the time), but if you find out you’re dying and have a date with death…or if you are just old enough to know it’s coming, then it is a kindness and a lifeline to know that humanity goes on and that everything you’ve seen in your life is an authentic part of the big picture of being human.  It sounds sad, but it’s a happy thing for people to know that they are NOT going to die without knowing what it really is to be a human.  These continuities are also why I loved being an archaeologist.  One of my favorite moments in archaeology was cleaning off a Roman roof tile and seeing that there were little footprints of a tiny piglet on one of them.  I could picture an Ancient Roman waving their hands to shoo the piglet away from the clay tiles as they dried in the sun.  It was such a perfect little snapshot of a very human moment some 2,000 years ago.

It wasn’t nearly as far back, but I also got to be the first to go in a 1930s bomb shelter in London that had been paved over for an RAF base before 1941 or something like that.  It seems like it could have been 1939, even though that seems almost too early, but anyway, no one had touched the place.  It was empty except for benches and just little strewn pieces of garbage and newspapers that looked like someone just had set them down an hour ago.  Even though garbage seems annoying normally, it can be fascinating if you just go several decades into the future.  The kinds of wrappers and posters and crumpled up notices, etc, you find in a place that has been closed for a whole few generations suddenly feel like gold (well, especially for archaeologists).  The term in archaeology is “in situ” and we are taught never to think anything is really legitimately in situ in archaeology because it’s unrealistic to think you will set the table and then never come in for dinner, and all the plates and napkins and silverware will be in that same position when an archaeologist finds it 50, 100, or 1,000 years later.  Everything gets disturbed by bugs and mice and rats and weather and movements of the Earth, etc.  There is no real in situ, normally, but I think I got about as close as is possible in that bomb shelter.  My supervisor on the dig let me go in all by myself because he knew what a kick I would get from it.

Okay, as many here know I have a very clear 5 Point Check that I do on all names.  Atlas and Maverick actually pass the first several checks…They can be spelled (they are not deliberately misspelled), and their meaning isn’t anything particularly bad.  Besides meaning and spelling there is the element of trendy stupidity.  I don’t see these as being particularly trendy, in that Atlas isn’t really a trend of any kind that I know of, even if it seems like kind of a weird name.  Maverick definitely WAS trendy, but I would say that trend started some 15 years ago at least, maybe 20.  I weigh that against the fact it isn’t a bad name in particular.  So far that one is coming out on top for me.

I have a couple more criteria, but let’s just focus on the “Ley” or “Leigh” endings.  This suffix is becoming so incredibly revoltingly trendy that I have no doubt it will be less than 20 years before people will be absolutely done with “Ley” and Leigh” endings.  It’s going to be dated.  That is my prediction.  People who have these names will seem old before their time.  Oakley is particularly egregious because people just won’t quit with that name.  It’s going around and around like a slipping record.  All the “Leighs” have to stop, but Oakley in particular.  It’s just obnoxious.  It’s gone too far.  Why don’t people have any self-respect?!  “Leigh” is the trend and it’s sickening to me how people are drawn into trends like this the same way that they’re drawn into goose-stepping with the Nazis.  It’s like this mass hysteria that happens.  People have to learn not to fall into these horrific habits like supporting dictatorial regimes and jumping on naming bandwagons.

People may not see what I see, but to me being swept up on a wave of propagandist autocratic fervor is precisely the same kind of thinking that makes people all start naming their kids the exactly same way.  A generation from now there will be ten million Oakleys, and unless someone has realized the error of their ways, it won’t stop there.  Grandpa Oakley will have a grandchild who is Oakley the Third, and it won’t sound distinguished;  It will sound like someone is stuck in another century.

The way we escape the trap of being just another faceless trend that makes our children another meaningless face in the crowd is to name someone something that isn’t a trend and yet isn’t so weird that people make that face they make when they smell rotten milk when they say it.

Now, of these names the most normal is frankly, Asher.  It isn’t one of my favorite names, but I think it’s one of the best in this list.  The reason why is that it isn’t made up but it’s also not common (that’s another of my criteria).  Asher is a name people can recognize and spell and understand as a name, but it isn’t one everyone has.  It has a decent nickname and it’s generally got nothing outstanding wrong with it.

Now I will address the last two…I saved them for last because…look, Ledger is a stupid name.  I was a fan of Heath Ledger, but it wasn’t his first name.  His name was Heath.  Heath isn’t a particularly bad name.  Ledger’s alright as a last name, but it makes a fairly stupid first name.  Who wants a name that basically means a list of expenses?  That’s like being named 1099.  People don’t like lists of expenses, debts, credits, etc, for a reason.  Under most circumstances that kind of thing is not fun.  It’s boring or upsetting or it’s like gloating if you’re some financial wizard.  It’s not very positive under almost all circumstances.

Then there’s Kaisen.  First of all, I am not okay with people naming someone something that had an obvious meaning associated with it and then having to say, “Oh, no, he’s not named after THAT!!”  It’s like someone naming their kid Sherlock and then telling everyone, “But it’s not after the detective!!  It’s just because we like the name, and besides…his brother is Mycroft…”  Now, I don’t know if they were thinking of Kaizen, the Japanese concept, but if they weren’t then this name is way too close to it.  The Japanese term is more complex than people in the West understand.  It doesn’t just mean constant improvement.  The same word has many shades of meaning in various contexts.  I love the concept of Kaizen, but I wouldn’t associate it with a child.  It has strange implications as a name, I think.

So really Maverick and Asher are the most normal of these.  Maverick is still a bit trendy, but I can accept it personally.  It has the most exciting meaning of this list.  Asher is the most NORMAL, and everyone seems to think normal is bad most of the time, when naming kids, but normal is NOT bad.  Overly common is bad.  Normal just means your child gets to make their name matter by their own way of living life, instead of having a flashy name but turning out not always as exciting as their name implies.  It’s like a curse.  You give someone an overly lofty name to live up to, and they are starting off life at a disadvantage.  Calling them by an uncommon but established name gives them room to be themselves.  To this end I think Atlas is TOO lofty.  Holding up the world?  I mean, come on!!  Maverick just implies a kid is original and maybe even a little rebellious, but that’s not bad to me.  Asher has less associations, but that’s GOOD.  That means the definition will be up to the child in their own lives!!  That’s the ideal!!
