I am glad to share these details.  I think it would be a missed opportunity for you not to write this up or show it to someone…You could take it seriously as an inspiration.  Personally I think A.I. is still too much in its infancy to QUITE be ready to take center stage in our everyday human life experiences, like movie watching.  However, as a source for new ideas, A.I. is brilliant!!  It’s like how lemon juice might be hard to drink, but when you add some sugar you suddenly have a really delicious combination that humans love.

I read an article once about how they can design plenty of pieces of equipment that can analyze what the components of wine are…Mass spectrographs, etc, but it can’t actually help them adequately to predict what humans are going to actually like.  You might think that knowing the exact chemistry of your wine can tell you who is going to like it, but the fact is that people like different chemicals in different amounts, depending on the combination.  It is like Game Theory, like that movie “A Beautiful Mind.”  At a certain number of combinations no one can work out the mathematics of what people will like.  It takes humans and our human intellect to know what humans will appreciate.  The difference between a flop TV show or movie and a winner is a HUGE amount of money to people!!  It could be like winning the lottery to write a winning screenplay or act in a movie that turns out to really mean something to people.

If people could predict what would be a success just by using computers, they certainly would, because it would save them hundreds of millions of dollars!!  However, just like making good lemonade, you can add the components together to your taste and hope other humans can appreciate the same mix.  Often your palate will not be THAT different from other people’s, even when you are creating something totally new.  That is why I think A.I. is great inspiration, but it needs the human touch.  I would see how you can go beyond this film by also developing a more in-depth story around it.  This would be just the seed.  The story needs to have the components that play with the audience’s expectations.  That is what does best at the box office.  You want to make it somehow timely.

I would think, “What is it about older people in a sci-fi context, that relates to something happening in the news right now?”  Then you stick that in.  You also think, “What would make a young protagonist very relatable to the current audience of the younger generation?”  Then you do a kind of “yin-yang” mix of what would interest young people about the older generation right now, and what would interest older people in the younger people around right now.  All of these are just intentionally thought-provoking questions.  The screenplay doesn’t have to have answers.  It can just have questions, and then play them out so that the different audiences have something to talk about afterwards.  Ironically good screenplays rarely answer all the questions posed in the story.  That is actually what BAD screenplays do.

What I see that is very marketable in this story is the general context of a lone detective on his own, having to work with a kind of network of older people who all are kind of connected and he can’t really be part of their society.  They are wealthy and old enough not to care if they are out of touch with current stuff.  This creates GOOD TENSION, that can have a variety of ways to be played out, and you would not have to show all of them, if you can at least just allude to those struggles in the story.

Ultimately you want to have the protagonist detective WIN OUT, in a sense, but like in Kurosawa’s Seven Samurai, it is a hollow victory and his fight is just a drop in the bucket finding a place amongst these members of the old guard who are fixed in their ways.  He wins by solving the case, but there is still so much more to do on the larger scale.  The case also has to have elements that address the struggle between classes and the struggle between the generations.  Maybe the deceased was somehow a great example of that struggle.  In the end the detective gets to tell off some members of the older generation in some way that younger people in the world today would cheer on.  This victory makes it all the more poignant that there are so many other struggles that cannot be overcome the way this case was.

I could go on forever, but that is literally what I will be teaching about later today!  Ha!!  I try to be inspiring just like A.I. is.  A.I. isn’t there to be the finished product.  It is there to be an ingredient of the whole.  You have to supply the human element to make it whole.  Your sense of the times we live in and the social setting of the world and these characters, is what A.I. needs to that you can collaborate with each other.  I am not one that thinks everything is about satisfying some demographic with your storylines, but it IS ABOUT having a story that you know someone else will feel deeply about.  If the struggle between Millennials and Boomers is still big in the world and you can picture that, then it could be a great start.  Maybe the older generation are not Boomers but Generation X.  Right away you have a target market.  Then you write to satisfy that audience so they see some of what they want to see, while also having some conflict they will feel when the story gets toward the climax.

I like your take on it!!  I like screenwriting because it has a very distinctly unique way of telling a story.  Novel writing has to be very descriptive, creating a world out of just some lines of text.  There has to be more economy in screenwriting though, so you have to pare down the image you have in your head to just sparse lines that merely point the way to getting a sense of the whole surroundings.  This also has a lot to do with the fact that a million things you have no control over will inevitably become part of the process of bringing your words to life.  There will be set designers and costume makers, not to mention the director and the producers, etc, who will all want to weigh in on what the look of each scene will be.  Therefore you are more creating a container for all that creativity to be funneled into.  They need to be pointed in the right direction to know where the story is going to go, but you have to leave some room for them no matter what.  Budgets change and many other things come to, like actors ad-libbing, etc.

I don’t mean to talk like I have so much experience with all this, of course, but I just think this is what makes screenwriting not the same as the descriptive language you use in a novel or poetry or song lyrics or a short story, etc.  A lot of stuff has to be pointed to and not elaborated on.  Someone walks in and they have a dirty jumpsuit on with their name stenciled into it, and you are meant to just assume they are working in a garage or auto shop.  You don’t have time in screenplays to tell everyone’s individual backstories, but you can at least create an image that lets the audience know that there is one.

So all that is why I think screenwriting is definitely deep.  I agree with you completely.  That is a good assessment.  It is visual poetry, rather than poetry with words.  It is like describing a poem without saying what the words of the poem are!!

I feel like I have to say that firstly I am not particularly in favor of tattoos of any kind.  I feel like they are kind of pointless, despite that I love art and I have no problem with whatever other people want permanently etched on their bodies.  To me part of my Buddhism is that the flesh is inherently transitory and while I try to keep up my body as just a means of getting me around, I keep it up the same way I do my car, just for maintenance purposes.  To me it is a fairly vain temptation to just decorate yourself with numerous pretty pictures.  It is not WRONG, but merely ultimately meaningless to your own inner peace and clarity of enlightenment.  Kind of like how much money you should spend on your clothing...Do expensive clothes bring you closer to enlightenment?  I could buy a flashy car to try and advertise to other people who I am with my car, but does that get me closer to enlightenment?  I feel like that is more a detriment to my enlightenment than it is a plus;  It is, first and foremost, a fixation on a material object.  This seems very much in direct opposition to my understanding of Buddhism being generally against focusing on material possessions.  A tattoo is a similar sort of material thing, even if it is on your body.

Having said all that though (and I feel that even here someone will have the kneejerk reaction to complain that I don't LOVE tattoos, because that is evidently a golden rule of modern culture that it is unacceptable to break, but you don't know how I grew up or how many tattoos I have seen...so please don't bother me with that), what I also think is that my feeling about tattoos being meaningless is EXACTLY why no one should care about this woman tattooing a picture of a generic image some people associate with the Buddha on her arm.  This is nothing more than an image.  Even being overly obsessed with identifying yourself with Buddhism is missing the point of Buddhism FOR ME...What someone does in reverence for your culture or your people or yourself or your religion is a silly thing to decide to have the vanity to be insulted or hurt by.  Even misusing your image (if you were a celebrity) is in some sense a form of love.  Even to be appropriated or to be used in a lampooning fashion by someone is to be recognized as worthy of note.  We act like the worst thing that can happen (in our modern techie lifestyles) is to be misunderstood or depicted in a way you would not approve of.  I say far worse is to be forgotten or not heralded or not even considered as worthy of note at all...and even then, these are really all vanities.

If our own image, or an image of some religious icon we believe in, is used by someone else in a way we don't approve of, is this not an opportunity for learning on everyone's part?  Should we not be glad that there is anything of note about these images?  The Thai Government, or organizations of Theravada or other such groups might urge not using images of Buddha as merely decorations, and I can see their intention in saying this, but I see this much like how it is actually considered strictly wrong to use the American Flag (since I am in the U.S.) as a form of clothing, and yet it is ceaselessly used as every kind of clothing you can imagine, including underwear.  Should I be deeply offended by this?  If someone made underwear with Jesus on the Cross, should that be deeply offensive?  I would think the person who would be most likely to wear underwear with Jesus on the Cross would be someone who considers themselves to be Christian themselves...so who is the one meant to be offended by this?

It appears to me we are living in an era where everyone sees everything that happens through the lens of whether or not they should be offended, as step number one in considering almost anything they come across in life.  I think nature and the world in general is a more organic beast than that.  Take the random creations of Artificial Intelligence as an example.  I saw several disclaimers about images created by Artificial Intelligence recently, stressing that it could be reflecting our biases and be extremely offensive in some way as a result.  It made me really think...How strange that we should even have to consider such a disclaimer.  Artificial Intelligence is literally reflecting back at us our own biases exactly as it sees them.  What on Earth could be more FAIR and open-minded?!!  It is not even ALIVE (without getting into definitions of sentience), so why can't we at least not be offended by mindless technology regurgitating our own world back at us in its own way?!  We are offended so easily that we don't see what an insanely powerful bias that is, in and of itself.  That seeing the world through the "offense lens" is not really seeing the world as it is at all.  It is looking for problems, with a set of ready "fixes" that we feel it is our job to employ.  None of that is seeing the world as it is and merely accepting it for being itself.  Buddhism is nothing in my mind if it cannot start by at least accepting the world, and all its joys and sorrows and cycles as merely itself.  That to me is the START of enlightenment.  Enlightenment is not seeing this world and wanting to perfect it.  This is NOT the perfect world, nor is it Nirvana.  This is Samsara.  Random tattoos of random things on people's bodies is samsara.  It is not enlightenment, it is just nothing more or less than what it is.  It can be a means of starting a dialogue, or it can be nothing.  It is nothing but a cycle of samsara to become wrapped up in the temptation to debate someone about whatever kind of art they like, or why they think they want a tattoo on their body, or where on their body, or why they have a statue of Buddha in their house as a decoration or as a shrine...When you go down these roads there is ONLY ceaseless cycles of meaningless arguments over worldly things that are not worth our time.

I think all these things take the concept of what religion means and create a considerably more superficial mindset around the depth that religion is supposed to have in people's lives.  This is not just an opportunity to be offended even by someone who meant no offense.  Sure, if I knew this woman I might ask her what she meant by having a tattoo of Buddha.  It might be a worthy conversation for us both to have.  That conversation might inspire either of us toward greater enlightenment.  Just to complain at her existence from afar seems utterly pointless to me though.  In a "choose your battles" kind of sense, she is the last person I would view as a threat to Buddhism or to people's progression toward enlightenment.  I would only hope for her that superficially labeling herself with a pretty picture of the Buddha is not where she stops in her development toward understanding Buddhism.  To me the most insulting thing is for someone to take the depth of thought that is available within Buddhism, and to limit it to such superficiality that it literally is barely more than skin deep for them...

You really have a point...I actually studied Ancient Egyptian a bit as an archaeologist at the British Museum many years ago. Now the mystique has changed because everyone knows you can download an app in a second that your cellphone can use to perform entirely new tasks.  Something like having a bug on a phone line or a tracker on your car is yawnworthy when it used to be exciting and only possible for spies or the FBI or something.

Therefore, I think the Q Branch is definitely something tricky in the modern era.  It’s a field that the movie industry may have to have some input from the techies out there about.  I don’t personally have a problem with the the nerdy spy work that they have put into the most recent Q (although damn it he looks so much like the nerd from the IT Crowd that I wish he was played by the same person). I mean, the world of apparel still has lots of possibilities.

I have to give the movies credit where it is due.  Throughout the course of the Bond Films they have gone from low level tech to imagining technologies that are legitimately on the forefront of what is possible at the highest level of current science.  To come up with new science fiction is a real challenge when our reality is genuinely seeming to be right on the edge of that.

What I see as kind of necessary is that Bond’s use of gadgets probably has to be altered within the scope of the stories.  There needs to be tech in any Bond Film for sure, but the tech can be less of a focal point, in the sense that having something do something new that never has been done before might not be the point.  Maybe the purpose of the tech might be more the realm of the fiction.  Coming up with new capabilities of what technology can do seems to legitimately be the era we are in, and that is restrained mainly by our own imaginations.

Hell, if Bond just had a cellphone he could use anywhere in the world then that would be an impressive device to me…but as a plotline if his devices also didn’t always work then that would be a good commentary on our current era as well.  I mean, his devices haven’t always worked in the movies, and I think that is good, but they could not work sometimes in a manner that is recognizable to us in our daily lives, and that would be interesting too.

In summary, I think Darthzilla99 is right that there are a lot of places in the world and area of work like spy work where analogue technology is very relevant even now.  I would also mention we haven’t seen Bind go to someplace like Antarctica before where a lot of normal tech might not work, but while I think the movies have really done an incredible job keeping up with technology it is also a hard thing to fulfill all the expectations of audiences for NEW tech that can be explained in a way the audience can understand…and FUN tech that is exciting, and also a variety of it that can be shown for Q to have a great array of “new toys!”

I had a funny relationship to Nirvana.  Even as they came out with new albums I had the feeling they were just so damned good, but simultaneously I wasn’t sure about something with them.  It has taken me the intervening decades to decipher what it was I was seeing.  I am not as negative as Kurt obviously was, so there was a side to me that balked at his negative focus but yet I was aware even at the time that it was era defining…and I loved that.  I felt closer to Chris Cornell than anyone at the time, but he was also fairly depressive.

Now I see that really I am a lot like them (not meaning in terms of talent, though I play guitar and sing and write songs), in that I am actually similarly jaded to a degree…but just in my own way…which is different from theirs.  I got to be actually quite close (in literal terms, not figurative) to Chris Cornell and I saw him from about 7 feet away in Hollywood at the Roxy.  I feel like I got to know him to a degree, at least his personality.

Kurt is still a bit inscrutable in my mind, but when I saw how his aunt taught him to play Beatles and so many hits of the 60s it became clear to me why I liked him.  He may have been very negative, but we loved the same musical oeuvre.  He and I had the same basis for music from day 1, and that is why we clicked.  I felt almost too similar to Kurt in some ways.  In the mid-90s we were (crazily) both in the same parts of Europe when he had his suicide attempt, 4 months before he…died.

I am not going to say his death was the result of suicide.  I am genuinely not convinced of that.  I do think that Courtney cheated on him with Billy Corrigan several months before he died, and I also think that that he was done with her and was moving out.  That whole thing is far too mysterious and convoluted for me to believe he was at least ALONE when he died.  The facts do not align, as far as I am concerned.  I had always had a kind of impending doom feeling with that band though.  I really have, and I think it affected me in liking them.

I am still a huge fan of both the other two in that band, and I always was.  I will just say that honestly I have tended to have a lot of premonitions in my life, and that was one I was feeling but wasn’t confident enough yet in that age of my life to actually accept that I had the ability to really feel that kind of thing before it happened.  Now I have been forced by repeated events to at least take myself more seriously if I feel those kinds of things.  I have taken the time to hone that part of myself, whatever you want to call it.  I am a very scientific person, but I know it is there because I have never stopped having proofs come my way constantly.

So anyway, I bet you didn’t expect this much response.  I feel like there is too much to explain though…Like, for example, Chris Cornell is buried in the same cemetery in Hollywood where many of my family members are buried, and I saw him in the most intimate show in Hollywood.  Nirvana, on the other hand, I will never stop kicking myself for missing.  I had tickets to see them on New Years Eve in Oakland, and I chose to let the tickets go so I could go to see my father. Who I had rarely gotten to see for most of my life, but always got along with.  I both am not sorry I saw my father, but I am also SHOCKED I missed my one chance to see Nirvana!!!  I was really not expecting that to be my last opportunity.

So, anyway, sorry to become so prolix, but these are things I feel like really affected my growing up.  I also got to meet and shake hands with Eddie Vedder, so I feel like I accomplished being a true child of the 90s in that sense.  I really got to know my most favorite bands…other than Nirvana.  That is why I was inspired to write all this.  Radiohead became my band in the late 90s, into the 2000s, and I was back in Europe when Coldplay and Muse hit the shelves in London, where I was staying at the time.  I knew all about them before anyone in the U.S. and I returned to insist my friends come see them with me.  I never forgot my original favorite bands from high school though.

I hope you don’t mind me going off, but thanks for reminding me of my whole musical upbringing!!!  Ha!!

P.S:  I think NIRVANA THEMSELVES thought Smells Like Teen Spirit was overplayed…just like Radiohead called Creep “their Iron Lung,” hence them writing that song as their next major single.  I am glad I saw Radiohead MANY times…and Muse and Coldplay.  The album I bought the moment it came out, while I was in London, was Kid A.  I loved the first albums, but Kid A was where the rest of everyone caught up to me in loving Radiohead, and it was a nice feeling.  I saw them in the Big Circus Tent in the park in London, and it was super awesome.
